# Electrolysis

## Core ideas and reasoning

Electrolysis uses electrical energy to drive a chemical change in a molten or dissolved electrolyte. Mobile ions carry current through the electrolyte; electrons carry current in external metal wires. Cations move toward the negative cathode and gain electrons by reduction. Anions move toward the positive anode and lose electrons by oxidation. In molten binary salts identify products from the two ions. In aqueous solutions water-derived species also compete, so use reactivity, concentration and electrode material. Inert graphite or platinum differs from reactive copper electrodes. For aqueous copper(II) sulfate with copper electrodes, copper dissolves at the anode and deposits at the cathode, approximately maintaining solution concentration under suitable conditions. Balance both atoms and charge in half-equations. Product mass depends on charge passed and the electron-to-product ratio; do not infer a gas or metal solely from the sign of an electrode. Describe observations separately from half-equations.

## Worked practice

### Example 1

Write the cathode half-equation for molten lead(II) bromide.

Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb. Lead ions gain electrons, so this is reduction.

### Example 2

Write the anode half-equation for molten lead(II) bromide.

2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻. Bromide ions lose electrons, so this is oxidation. Atom and charge totals balance.

### Example 3

What happens to a copper anode in electrolysis of aqueous copper(II) sulfate using copper electrodes?

It dissolves as Cu(s) → Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻, losing mass while supplying copper ions to the solution.

## Check your reasoning

Explain why the method applies before calculating or naming a result. Compare with a contrasting case. For calculations carry units, keep intermediate precision, then check by substitution, conservation or a second route. Describe observations separately from their explanation.
